title: Describing with adjectives
topic: agreement and position of adjectives; très and beaucoup
why: This lesson teaches you to describe: adjectives that agree in gender and number, that mostly come after the noun, and the short group (beau, petit, vieux…) that comes before it. With très and beaucoup, you can now describe your city, your apartment and the things around you.

{"lessons": ["

Adjectives agree

In English, an adjective never changes: “a big house”, “big houses”. In French, it agrees in gender and number with the noun, exactly like the nationalities you already know. The basic rule: add -e for the feminine, -s for the plural.

masculinefeminine
singularil est grandelle est grande
pluralils sont grandselles sont grandes

Listen to the feminine: the -e makes the final consonant heard. petit ends on “ee”, petite on a clear t; gris / grise, grand / grande. The plural -s, as always, is silent.

Other patterns

patternmasculine → feminineexample
already ends in -eno changerouge, facile, moderne, jeune
-eux → -euseheureux → heureusehappy
-if → -ivesportif → sportiveathletic, sporty
-ien → -ienneancien → ancienneold, former
-er → -èrecher → chèreexpensive

In the plural, a few endings are special: an adjective in -s or -x doesn't change (gris, heureux: ils sont heureux), and -al becomes -aux in the masculine plural (normal → normaux).

La voiture est petite, mais elle est chère.The car is small, but it's expensive.

For a mixed group, use the masculine plural: Léa et Hugo sont sportifs.

", "

Where does the adjective go?

Here French reverses English: most adjectives come after the noun. “A red car” is une voiture rouge, “a modern apartment” is un appartement moderne. Colors, shapes, nationalities and most long adjectives always go after.

J'habite dans un appartement moderne, dans une rue calme.I live in a modern apartment, on a quiet street.

But a small group of very common, short adjectives come before the noun. A trick to remember them: beauty, age, goodness, size.

meaningadjectives (masculine / feminine)example
beautybeau / belle, joli / jolieune jolie ville
agejeune, vieux / vieille, nouveau / nouvelleun nouveau professeur
goodnessbon / bonne, mauvais / mauvaiseun bon café
sizegrand / grande, petit / petite, gros / grosseune grande maison

Bel, nouvel, vieil

Before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or silent h, three of them have a special form, to link the sounds: un bel appartement, un nouvel ami, un vieil hôtel. They sound like the feminine belle, nouvelle, vieille.

masculinebefore a vowelfeminine
un beau parcun bel appartementune belle ville
un nouveau muséeun nouvel hôpitalune nouvelle école
un vieux quartierun vieil amiune vieille rue

In the plural, des before an adjective often becomes de in careful French: de belles rues. You'll hear des belles rues too; just recognize it for now.

", "

Très and beaucoup

English uses “very” and “a lot” in different places, and French does too, but learners mix them up constantly.

wordwithexample
très (very)an adjectiveLa ville est très belle.
beaucoup (a lot, very much)a verb, right after itJ'aime beaucoup Bordeaux.
beaucoup de (a lot of, many)a noun, with no articleIl y a beaucoup de cafés.

Never say “très beaucoup”: beaucoup already means “very much”. And after beaucoup de, no le, la, les or des: beaucoup de touristes, beaucoup d'amis.

Describing your city or your apartment

With être, c'est and il y a, you can now paint a full picture:

J'habite à Bordeaux. C'est une très belle ville. Il y a beaucoup de vieilles rues et de jolis cafés.I live in Bordeaux. It's a very beautiful city. There are lots of old streets and pretty cafés.
L'appartement est petit, mais il est moderne et très calme. J'aime beaucoup le quartier.The apartment is small, but it's modern and very quiet. I really like the neighborhood.

Notice: after c'est + a noun, the adjective agrees with the noun (c'est une belle ville); but alone after c'est, it stays masculine (Bordeaux ? C'est beau !).

Cher before or after? After: un appartement cher = an expensive apartment. Before, in a letter, Chère Léa means “Dear Léa”.
